prime.problem: An 8-GPU job at the head of the queue waits for GPUs to free up, and the free ones sit idle meanwhile. And a distributed job placed one pod at a time can end up holding GPUs while waiting for the rest of itself, with nothing training at all.
prime.fits: Second case-study card. It builds on the fair-share card (whose task-at-a-time model breaks for big jobs) and on cs-7's deadlock conditions; the next card turns these waits into something a user can understand.
expect: the shadow time and extra GPUs
prime.goal: Run EASY backfilling by hand on a small queue, compute waits and idle GPU-hours, and explain why gang placement prevents hoarding deadlocks.

attend: What is the shadow time, and why is it computed from when running jobs end rather than from the queue?
Why does J2 backfill at t = 0 while J3, which also needs only 2 GPUs, has to wait?
Why does the greedy policy have the best average wait on this example, yet the card rejects it?
In the four-machine example, which Coffman conditions for deadlock are present when every job holds one learner?
Why does backfilling depend on users' runtime estimates, and what happens when they're wrong?

must: The head job can't fit → reserve its earliest start (the shadow time, when running jobs free enough GPUs) → a later job may start now only if it ends by the shadow time or uses GPUs the head won't need → holes are filled without delaying the head
Without a reservation, anything that fits starts → small jobs keep taking freed GPUs → the big job slips (J1 4 → 6 h here) and may starve under steady small arrivals

A distributed job needs all its learners at once → placing pods one at a time can give every job half → all GPUs held, no job trains, until timeouts (hold-and-wait) → gang placement starts a whole job or none
Gang placement makes a big job wait for a large free block → GPUs idle while it accumulates → backfilling is what fills that gap
elevated: Decisions use submitted time limits → a job that runs past its limit is killed → padded estimates still work (early finishes open new holes), per Mu'alem and Feitelson
reference: EASY vs conservative naming and Slurm's backfill wording
the sweep-depth cap in real schedulers
the O(q·r log r) pass cost

compress.prompt: Close the card. Write the EASY rule with shadow and extra, then the waits table for FCFS, EASY and greedy on J1–J4 with average waits and idle GPU-hours before t = 4. One sentence on what gang placement prevents.
checklist: shadow = when enough GPUs free for the head; extra = GPUs free then minus the head's need
start j now if it fits and (ends by shadow or fits in extra)
FCFS 5.5 h / 16 idle GPU-h; EASY 4.0 h / 10; greedy 2.5 h / 2, but J1 slips to t = 6
the head job still starts at its reservation under EASY
gang: all learners or none, so no partial holds and no temporary deadlock

retrieve.q: Explain what EASY backfilling protects and what it doesn't, compared with conservative backfilling.
answer: EASY protects only the head job's reserved start
conservative protects every job ahead of the candidate
EASY fills more holes; conservative gives more jobs predictable starts

retrieve.q: Walk through the EASY decisions at t = 0 and t = 3 for the card's queue.
answer: t = 0: 4 free; J1 needs 8, reserve at shadow t = 4, extra 0
J3: 0 + 6 > 4 and 2 > extra, waits; J4 needs 4, only 2 left
t = 3: J2 ends; J4 would end at 5 > 4 and J3 at 9 > 4, both wait; J1 starts at 4

retrieve.q: Your cluster runs mostly long training jobs with unknown runtimes. Argue how much backfilling will help, and what you'd do instead or in addition.
answer: backfilling needs estimates to know what ends by the shadow time
with unknown or very long runtimes few jobs qualify, so little is filled
require time limits, reserve and gang-place, and prefer checkpointable jobs for preemption

compare.q: Fair share decides who gets the next GPUs; backfilling decides which job may use idle ones now. How do the two interact, and what goes wrong if you use only one?
answer: fair share orders the queue by users' entitlements
backfill fills holes left by a blocked head without delaying it
only fair share: big jobs block and GPUs idle
only backfill: one user's small jobs can dominate the holes

compare.q: The partial-gang deadlock and cs-7's lock deadlock: which Coffman conditions appear in each, and which one does gang placement remove?
answer: both: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a wait cycle (each job waits on GPUs another holds)
gang placement removes hold-and-wait: a job holds nothing until it gets everything
lock ordering removes the cycle instead

predict.q: J2 said 3 hours but actually runs 5, and this scheduler doesn't kill jobs at their limit. Commit first: when does J1 start under EASY, and what does that say about enforcing time limits?
predict.answer: J1 needs all 8 GPUs. At t = 4, J0 frees its 4, but J2 still holds 2 until t = 5, so J1 starts at t = 5, one hour past its reservation. Backfilling is only safe for the head job if backfilled jobs can't overrun, which is why schedulers kill at the time limit (or preempt).

apply.task: Change J2's estimate to 5 hours (still 2 GPUs) and rerun EASY by hand: which job backfills at t = 0 now, when does each job start, the average wait, and the idle GPU-hours before t = 4. Check by editing QUEUE in code/backfill-gang-scheduling.py.
apply.done: J2 no longer fits the window (0 + 5 > 4), but J4 does: 4 GPUs free and 0 + 2 ≤ 4, so J4 starts at 0. Starts: J1 4, J2 6, J3 6, J4 0; average wait 16/4 = 4.0 h; idle GPU-hours before t = 4: 32 − 16 − 4 × 2 = 8.
apply.hint: Check every queued job behind the head at t = 0, not just the next one.
